analysis.one_liner: Bars exports of US-produced crude oil and natural gas to keep energy at home.
analysis.headline: The bill to restore the oil and gas export ban never left committee; it died without a vote after the 2023-24 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have reinstated the ban on exporting crude oil, which Congress lifted in 2015, and added a ban on exporting natural gas. The President would have been required to write rules prohibiting those exports, with narrow exemptions if the national interest demanded. The goal was to keep American energy supplies and the equipment that produces them inside the United States instead of selling them abroad. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be American households and businesses relying on domestic fuel, since crude and gas produced here could no longer be sold overseas in unlimited amounts, and domestic refiners, who would keep first claim on cheap domestic crude as feedstock.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require the President to issue a rule prohibiting export of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, with exemptions only where the President finds them consistent with the national interest.

It also gives the President discretionary authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, petrochemical feedstocks, and even energy-related equipment and supplies, with penalties enforced under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018.
The restrictions must account for existing trade arrangements with Canada and Mexico and cross-border transport conveniences, softening the disruption to North American energy trade.
The President may waive the usual notice-and-comment period only if delay would seriously impair the ability to impose effective and timely export prohibitions.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and the LNG export industry would lose their overseas markets, which would reduce export revenues and likely lead to less domestic drilling. Trading partners that buy American energy could also retaliate against other US exports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and LNG exporters

drawbacks.text: Reinstating an export ban could reduce drillers' revenue enough to slow US oil and gas production, which over time could cut supply and raise prices for the very consumers the bill is meant to protect — the opposite of its stated goal.

Blocking crude exports also removes incentive to keep domestic prices aligned with world markets; when domestic supply exceeds refinery capacity, producers would have to discount output, and some analysts argue the 2015 export lift actually lowered gasoline prices for consumers rather than raising them.

A broad export restriction on coal, petroleum products, and energy equipment would give the President sweeping trade power with few constraints, and could invite retaliation against other American exports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's aim — keep domestic energy home when prices spike — has real intuitive appeal, but its economic effect is genuinely contested: an export ban can lower some consumer prices in the short run while also shrinking production incentives that keep domestic supply high. It also hands the President broad discretion over energy trade, which is a serious concentration of power even with the Canada and Mexico carve-outs. The bill never got a hearing, so these tradeoffs were never tested in public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy, Climate and Grid Security Subcommittee the day after introduction, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Adriano Espaillat introduced the BAN Fossil Fuel Exports Act on May 18, 2023, to reinstate a ban on crude oil and natural gas exports.
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on May 18, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security on May 19, 2023.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and LNG export companies are better off, since their unlimited access to overseas markets was never threatened; the committee's inaction meant the bill never even came up for debate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

for.name: Rep. Adriano Espaillat
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the crude oil and natural gas export ban.

for.name: 7 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; original cosponsors included Reps. Yvette Clarke, Jared Huffman, and Julia Brownley.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral; it stayed in the Energy, Climate and Grid Security Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it had no path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 supporters were Democrats — the sponsor plus 7 cosponsors — and no Republican supported it in the Republican-controlled House, so the bill had no bipartisan path.

industries.industry: Crude oil and natural gas producers
industries.note: A mandatory export ban would cut off overseas sales and lower the value of domestic production, likely reducing drilling. Producers' interest in keeping export access ran against the bill's consumer-protection rationale.
A natural gas export ban would end the export business that built terminals on the Gulf Coast; the industry's revenue depends on shipping US gas abroad.
Keeping crude oil at home would guarantee refiners first access to domestic feedstock at potentially lower cost, but they could face retaliation abroad and reduced product export markets.
The bill gives the President discretionary power to restrict coal exports, a threat to the industry's overseas sales, though not a mandatory ban.
